question: Air brakes are actually three different braking systems combined. Which of the following is NOT one of the three?
choice_a: Service brake system
choice_b: Parking brake system
choice_c: Emergency brake system
choice_d: Auxiliary brake system
explanation: Air brakes consist of the service brake, parking brake, and emergency brake systems; there is no separate 'auxiliary brake system' in this framework.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5, Air Brakes (introduction)

question: Which air brake system applies and releases the brakes when you use the brake pedal during normal driving?
choice_a: The parking brake system
choice_b: The service brake system
choice_c: The emergency brake system
choice_d: The spring brake system
explanation: The service brake system applies and releases the brakes when the brake pedal is used during normal driving.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5, Air Brakes (introduction)

question: How is the air compressor typically connected to power it in a commercial vehicle?
choice_a: It is powered by a separate electric motor
choice_b: It is connected to the engine through gears or a v-belt
choice_c: It is powered by the hydraulic system
choice_d: It is powered directly by the transmission
explanation: The air compressor pumps air into the air storage tanks and is connected to the engine through gears or a v-belt.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.1, Air Compressor

question: About what air pressure causes the governor to stop the compressor from pumping air (the 'cut-out' level)?
choice_a: Around 80 psi
choice_b: Around 100 psi
choice_c: Around 125 psi
choice_d: Around 150 psi
explanation: The governor stops the compressor from pumping air when tank pressure rises to the 'cut-out' level, around 125 psi.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.2, Air Compressor Governor

question: When air tank pressure falls to the 'cut-in' pressure of around 100 psi, what does the governor do?
choice_a: It shuts off the engine
choice_b: It opens the safety relief valve
choice_c: It allows the compressor to start pumping air again
choice_d: It applies the spring brakes
explanation: When tank pressure falls to the cut-in pressure (around 100 psi), the governor allows the compressor to start pumping again.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.2, Air Compressor Governor

question: What is the purpose of the air storage tanks (reservoirs) in an air brake system?
choice_a: To cool the compressed air before it reaches the brakes
choice_b: To hold compressed air so brakes can be used several times even if the compressor stops working
choice_c: To filter oil out of the engine
choice_d: To power the parking brake control only
explanation: Air storage tanks hold compressed air and will hold enough to allow the brakes to be used several times even if the compressor stops working.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.3, Air Storage Tanks

question: Why is it important to drain air tanks that use manually operated drain valves?
choice_a: Because water and compressor oil collect in the tank and can freeze and cause brake failure in cold weather
choice_b: Because draining increases the governor cut-out pressure
choice_c: Because it recharges the alcohol evaporator
choice_d: Because it resets the ABS malfunction lamp
explanation: Compressed air usually has water and compressor oil in it; this can freeze in cold weather and cause brake failure, so tanks with manual drain valves must be drained completely by the driver at the end of each day.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.4, Air Tank Drains

question: What is the purpose of an alcohol evaporator in some air brake systems?
choice_a: To lubricate the fifth wheel
choice_b: To reduce the risk of ice forming in air brake valves and other parts during cold weather
choice_c: To clean the brake linings
choice_d: To increase the governor cut-out pressure
explanation: An alcohol evaporator puts alcohol into the air system to help reduce the risk of ice in air brake valves and other parts during cold weather.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.5, Alcohol Evaporator

question: The safety relief valve installed in the first tank the air compressor pumps to is usually set to open at about what pressure?
choice_a: 100 psi
choice_b: 125 psi
choice_c: 150 psi
choice_d: 200 psi
explanation: The safety relief valve protects the tank and system from too much pressure and is usually set to open at 150 psi; if it releases air, something is wrong and a mechanic should fix the fault.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.6, Safety Valve

question: The air brake pedal is also known by what other names?
choice_a: The trolley valve or Johnson bar
choice_b: The foot valve or treadle valve
choice_c: The modulating valve or dash control
choice_d: The tractor protection valve
explanation: The brake pedal is also called the foot valve or treadle valve; pushing it down harder applies more air pressure.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.7, The Brake Pedal

question: Why should a driver avoid pressing and releasing the brake pedal unnecessarily?
choice_a: It can let air out of the system faster than the compressor can replace it, and if pressure gets too low the brakes won't work
choice_b: It causes the alcohol evaporator to overfill
choice_c: It permanently disables the ABS system
choice_d: It voids the vehicle's warranty
explanation: Releasing the brakes lets compressed air out of the system, reducing tank pressure; pressing and releasing the pedal unnecessarily can deplete air faster than the compressor can replace it, and if pressure gets too low the brakes won't work.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.7, The Brake Pedal

question: What is the most common type of foundation brake used at each wheel on air-braked vehicles?
choice_a: Disc brake
choice_b: Wedge brake
choice_c: S-cam drum brake
choice_d: Hydraulic drum brake
explanation: The most common type of foundation brake is the s-cam drum brake.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.8, Foundation Brakes

question: In an s-cam brake, what happens when air pressure pushes the brake chamber push rod out?
choice_a: It moves the slack adjuster, twisting the brake camshaft and turning the s-cam, which forces the brake shoes against the drum
choice_b: It directly clamps the rotor between brake pads
choice_c: It releases air from the emergency line
choice_d: It opens the tractor protection valve
explanation: Air pressure pushes the rod out, moving the slack adjuster and twisting the brake camshaft, which turns the s-shaped cam; the s-cam forces the brake shoes apart and against the inside of the brake drum.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.8, Foundation Brakes (S-cam Brakes)

question: How do wedge brakes apply braking force?
choice_a: A power screw clamps the disc between brake lining pads like a c-clamp
choice_b: The brake chamber push rod pushes a wedge directly between the ends of two brake shoes, shoving them apart against the drum
choice_c: A rotating cam twists a camshaft to spread brake shoes
choice_d: Compressed air directly contacts the brake drum
explanation: In wedge brakes, the brake chamber push rod pushes a wedge directly between the ends of two brake shoes, shoving them apart and against the inside of the brake drum.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.8, Foundation Brakes (Wedge Brakes)

question: In air-operated disc brakes, what part is used instead of the s-cam to clamp the disc?
choice_a: A wedge
choice_b: A modulating valve
choice_c: A power screw
choice_d: A trolley valve
explanation: In air-operated disc brakes, a 'power screw' is used instead of an s-cam; the brake chamber's pressure on the slack adjuster turns the power screw, which clamps the disc between brake lining pads of a caliper, similar to a large c-clamp.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.8, Foundation Brakes (Disc Brakes)

question: On a vehicle with a dual air brake system, how many supply pressure gauges (or gauge needles) are provided?
choice_a: None; dual systems have no supply gauge
choice_b: One gauge for the whole vehicle regardless of system
choice_c: A gauge (or needle) for each half of the system
choice_d: Three gauges, one per axle
explanation: If the vehicle has a dual air brake system, there will be a gauge for each half of the system, or a single gauge with two needles, telling how much pressure is in the air tanks.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.9, Supply Pressure Gauges

question: What does it mean if you need to apply increasing application pressure to hold the same speed?
choice_a: The alcohol evaporator is empty
choice_b: The brakes are fading, and you should slow down and use a lower gear
choice_c: The ABS system has malfunctioned
choice_d: The governor cut-in pressure is too low
explanation: Increasing application pressure needed to hold the same speed means the brakes are fading; the driver should slow down and use a lower gear, as this can also be caused by brakes out of adjustment, air leaks, or mechanical problems.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.10, Application Pressure Gauge

question: By what point must a visible low air pressure warning signal come on in a vehicle with air brakes?
choice_a: Before the air pressure in the tanks falls below 55 psi
choice_b: Before the air pressure falls below 100 psi
choice_c: Only after the spring brakes have already applied
choice_d: Before the air pressure falls below 125 psi
explanation: A warning signal you can see must come on before the air pressure in the tanks falls below 55 psi (or one half the compressor governor cutout pressure on older vehicles); the warning is usually a red light and a buzzer may also sound.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.11, Low Air Pressure Warning

question: What is the 'wig wag' warning device on some air brake systems?
choice_a: An electronic voice alert
choice_b: A mechanical arm that drops into the driver's view when system pressure drops below 55 psi
choice_c: A dashboard light that only illuminates at start-up
choice_d: A horn that sounds continuously
explanation: The wig wag device drops a mechanical arm into the driver's view when pressure in the system drops below 55 psi; an automatic wig wag rises out of view when pressure rises back above 55 psi, while a manual reset type must be placed out of view by hand.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.11, Low Air Pressure Warning

question: How does the air brake system turn on the brake lights when the driver applies the air brakes?
choice_a: Through a mechanical cable linked to the brake pedal
choice_b: Through an electric switch that works by air pressure
choice_c: Through the ABS malfunction lamp circuit
choice_d: Through the parking brake control knob
explanation: The air brake system warns drivers behind with an electric switch that works by air pressure; the switch turns on the brake lights when the air brakes are applied.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.12, Stop Light Switch

question: According to the manual, what does testing show about front wheel braking, even on ice?
choice_a: Front wheel skids from braking are not likely, so the limiting valve control should be kept in the 'normal' position for full stopping power
choice_b: Front wheel brakes should always be disabled on ice
choice_c: The 'slippery' position always improves stopping distance
choice_d: Front brakes are illegal on vehicles made after 1975
explanation: Tests have shown front wheel skids from braking are not likely even on ice; front wheel braking is good under all conditions, so the control should be in the 'normal' position for normal stopping power, since the 'slippery' setting on older vehicles actually reduces stopping power.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.13, Front Brake Limiting Valve

question: Why are spring brakes used to meet the requirement that trucks, truck tractors, and buses have emergency and parking brakes held on by mechanical force?
choice_a: Because air pressure can eventually leak away, so mechanical spring force is needed to hold the brakes on reliably
choice_b: Because springs are cheaper than air chambers
choice_c: Because federal law requires hydraulic backup on all CMVs
choice_d: Because springs allow higher top speeds
explanation: Parking and emergency brakes must be held on by mechanical force because air pressure can eventually leak away; spring brakes use powerful springs held back by air pressure, and if air pressure is removed the springs put on the brakes.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.14, Spring Brakes

question: On tractors and straight trucks, spring brakes will typically come fully on when air pressure drops to what range?
choice_a: 0 to 10 psi
choice_b: 20 to 45 psi (typically 20 to 30 psi)
choice_c: 55 to 80 psi
choice_d: 100 to 125 psi
explanation: Tractor and straight truck spring brakes will come fully on when air pressure drops to a range of 20 to 45 psi, typically 20 to 30 psi; drivers should not wait for this and should stop safely when the low air warning first activates.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.14, Spring Brakes

question: Why should a driver never push the brake pedal down while the spring brakes are already on?
choice_a: It has no effect either way
choice_b: It could damage the brakes from the combined forces of the springs and the air pressure
choice_c: It automatically releases the spring brakes
choice_d: It engages the tractor protection valve
explanation: Never push the brake pedal down when the spring brakes are on, because the brakes could be damaged by the combined forces of the springs and the air pressure; not all brake systems are designed to prevent this.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.14, Spring Brakes

question: On newer vehicles with air brakes, how is the parking brake control typically shaped and colored?
choice_a: A round blue knob
choice_b: A diamond-shaped, yellow, push-pull control knob
choice_c: A square red button
choice_d: A green toggle switch
explanation: On newer vehicles with air brakes, you put on the parking brakes using a diamond-shaped, yellow, push-pull control knob; pulling it out applies the spring brakes, and pushing it in releases them.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.15, Parking Brake Controls

question: What is a modulating control valve used for on some vehicles with spring brakes?
choice_a: To apply the spring brakes gradually, giving the driver a feel for the braking action if the service brakes fail
choice_b: To drain the alcohol evaporator
choice_c: To switch between primary and secondary air systems
choice_d: To control the fifth wheel release handle
explanation: A modulating control valve on the dashboard lets the driver apply the spring brakes gradually; it is spring-loaded so the driver has a feel for the braking action, allowing control of the spring brakes if the service brakes fail.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.15, Parking Brake Controls (Modulating Control Valves)

question: Truck tractors with air brakes built on or after what date are required to be equipped with antilock brakes (ABS)?
choice_a: March 1, 1994
choice_b: March 1, 1997
choice_c: March 1, 1998
choice_d: March 1, 2000
explanation: Truck tractors with air brakes built on or after March 1, 1997 are required to be equipped with ABS; other air brake vehicles (trucks, buses, trailers, converter dollies) built on or after March 1, 1998 have the same requirement.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.16, Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: What color are the ABS malfunction lamps required on vehicles equipped with antilock brakes?
choice_a: Red
choice_b: Green
choice_c: Yellow
choice_d: Blue
explanation: Vehicles with ABS have yellow malfunction lamps to indicate if something isn't working; tractors, trucks, and buses have them on the instrument panel, while trailers have them on the left side, front or rear corner.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.16, Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: Does ABS decrease or increase a vehicle's normal braking capability?
choice_a: It decreases normal braking capability to prevent skids
choice_b: It increases normal braking capability at all times
choice_c: It does neither; ABS only activates when wheels are about to lock up and does not change normal braking capability
choice_d: It replaces the need for normal service brakes entirely
explanation: ABS is an addition to normal brakes; it does not decrease or increase normal braking capability and only activates when wheels are about to lock up.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.1.16, Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: What is a dual air brake system?
choice_a: A system with two air compressors but one set of brake controls
choice_b: Two separate air brake systems that use a single set of brake controls, each with its own tanks, hoses, and lines
choice_c: A single air system with two safety valves
choice_d: A backup hydraulic system paired with an air system
explanation: A dual air brake system has two separate air brake systems, which use a single set of brake controls; each system has its own air tanks, hoses, and lines, with one system typically operating the rear brakes (primary) and the other the front brakes (secondary).
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.2, Dual Air Brake

question: Before driving a vehicle with a dual air system, what minimum pressure should be allowed to build up in both the primary and secondary systems?
choice_a: 55 psi
choice_b: 75 psi
choice_c: 100 psi
choice_d: 125 psi
explanation: Before driving a vehicle with a dual air system, the driver should allow time for the air compressor to build up a minimum of 100 psi pressure in both the primary and secondary systems.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.2, Dual Air Brake

question: In a dual air brake system, at what point must the low air pressure warning light and buzzer come on?
choice_a: Before the air pressure drops below 55 psi in either system
choice_b: Only after both systems drop below 20 psi
choice_c: Only when the parking brake is applied
choice_d: Before the air pressure drops below 100 psi in both systems
explanation: The warning light and buzzer should come on before the air pressure drops below 55 psi in either the primary or secondary system; if this happens while driving, the vehicle should be stopped and parked safely right away.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.2, Dual Air Brake

question: When checking slack adjusters on s-cam brakes during a walk-around inspection, what movement at the push rod indicates the slack adjuster probably needs adjustment?
choice_a: Any movement at all
choice_b: Movement of more than about one inch where the push rod attaches to it
choice_c: Movement of exactly one-quarter inch
choice_d: No movement whatsoever
explanation: With the parking brakes released, if a slack adjuster moves more than about one inch where the push rod attaches to it, it probably needs adjustment; out-of-adjustment brakes are the most common problem found in roadside inspections.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.3.2, Walk-around Inspection (Slack Adjusters)

question: Vehicles built since 1994 have automatic slack adjusters. Do these still need to be checked?
choice_a: No, automatic slack adjusters never need checking
choice_b: Yes, even though they adjust themselves during full brake applications, they must still be checked
choice_c: Only if the vehicle is a combination vehicle
choice_d: Only once per year during annual inspection
explanation: Even though automatic slack adjusters adjust themselves during full brake applications, they must still be checked; manual adjustment of an automatic adjuster should only be used as a temporary emergency measure, since it usually does not fix the underlying problem.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.3.2, Walk-around Inspection (Slack Adjusters)

question: During a brake drum or disc inspection, what crack length is a cause for concern?
choice_a: Any crack, no matter how small
choice_b: Cracks longer than one half the width of the friction area
choice_c: Cracks longer than the full diameter of the drum
choice_d: Only cracks visible without removing the wheel
explanation: Brake drums (or discs) must not have cracks longer than one half the width of the friction area; linings must not be loose, soaked with oil or grease, or dangerously thin.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.3.2, Walk-around Inspection (Brake Drums, Linings, and Hoses)

question: During the Step 7 final air brake check, about what pressures should the governor cut the air compressor in and out?
choice_a: Cut-in about 50 psi, cut-out about 75 psi
choice_b: Cut-in about 100 psi, cut-out about 125 psi
choice_c: Cut-in about 125 psi, cut-out about 150 psi
choice_d: Cut-in about 20 psi, cut-out about 45 psi
explanation: Pumping by the air compressor should start (cut-in) at about 100 psi and stop (cut-out) at about 125 psi, checked against the manufacturer's specifications while running the engine at a fast idle.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: With a fully charged air system, engine off, and parking brake released, what is the maximum allowable static air leakage rate for a single vehicle?
choice_a: Less than one psi in one minute
choice_b: Less than two psi in one minute
choice_c: Less than three psi in one minute
choice_d: Less than five psi in one minute
explanation: For a fully-charged air system with the engine off and parking brake released, the static loss rate should be less than two psi in one minute for single vehicles (less than three psi in one minute for combination vehicles).
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check (Test Air Leakage Rate)

question: When holding the foot brake fully applied for one minute during the final air brake check, how much air pressure drop is allowed for a single vehicle before the air loss rate is considered too much?
choice_a: More than three pounds in one minute
choice_b: More than five pounds in one minute
choice_c: More than one pound in one minute
choice_d: More than ten pounds in one minute
explanation: With the foot brake fully applied and held for one minute, if the air pressure falls more than three psi in one minute for single vehicles (more than four psi for combination vehicles), the air loss rate is too much and leaks must be found and fixed before driving.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check

question: In a dual air system at operating rpm, the air pressure should build from 85 to 100 psi within how many seconds?
choice_a: 15 seconds
choice_b: 30 seconds
choice_c: 45 seconds
choice_d: 90 seconds
explanation: When the engine is at operating rpms, the pressure should build from 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds in dual air systems; if a vehicle has larger than minimum air tanks, the buildup time can be longer and still be safe per the manufacturer's specifications.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check (Check Rate of Air Pressure Buildup)

question: How should a driver test that spring brakes come on automatically during the final air brake check?
choice_a: By fanning off air pressure with the brake pedal until the parking brake valve pops out at the manufacturer's specified pressure, typically 20-45 psi
choice_b: By checking the safety valve opens at 150 psi
choice_c: By driving at highway speed and applying the parking brake
choice_d: By disconnecting the emergency line
explanation: By continuing to fan off air pressure by stepping on and off the brake pedal, the parking brake valve (and tractor protection valve on a combination vehicle) should close, or pop out, when air pressure falls to the manufacturer's specification, typically 20-45 psi, causing the spring brakes to come on.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check (Check That Spring Brakes Come On Automatically)

question: What is the added delay called that occurs with air brakes, representing the time required for the brakes to work after the brake pedal is pushed?
choice_a: Reaction distance
choice_b: Brake lag
choice_c: Perception distance
choice_d: Governor delay
explanation: With air brakes there is an added delay called 'brake lag,' the time required for the brakes to work after the brake pedal is pushed, unlike hydraulic brakes which work almost instantly.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.4.4, Stopping Distance

question: At 55 mph on dry pavement, about how much distance does air brake lag add, and what is the resulting total stopping distance for an average driver under good conditions?
choice_a: About 10 feet, totaling over 300 feet
choice_b: About 32 feet, totaling over 450 feet
choice_c: About 100 feet, totaling over 600 feet
choice_d: About 5 feet, totaling over 250 feet
explanation: The air brake lag distance at 55 mph on dry pavement adds about 32 feet; total stopping distance (perception + reaction + brake lag + braking distance) for an average driver under good traction and brake conditions is over 450 feet.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.4.4, Stopping Distance

question: What is the 'controlled braking' method for an emergency stop?
choice_a: Applying the brakes as hard as possible without locking the wheels, keeping steering movements small
choice_b: Applying the brakes all the way and releasing them only when wheels lock up
choice_c: Using the trailer hand valve to slow the vehicle
choice_d: Pumping the brake pedal rapidly at highway speed
explanation: With controlled braking, the driver applies the brakes as hard as possible without locking the wheels, keeping steering wheel movements very small; if a larger steering adjustment is needed or the wheels lock, the driver releases and re-applies the brakes as soon as possible.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.4.3, Emergency Stops (Controlled Braking)

question: What is the 'stab braking' method for an emergency stop?
choice_a: Applying brakes all the way, releasing when wheels lock, then reapplying fully once the wheels start rolling again
choice_b: Applying light, steady pressure throughout the stop
choice_c: Using only the trailer hand valve
choice_d: Downshifting without touching the brake pedal
explanation: With stab braking, the driver applies the brakes all the way, releases them when the wheels lock up, and applies the brakes fully again as soon as the wheels start rolling; it can take up to one second for wheels to start rolling after release, and reapplying too soon prevents the vehicle from straightening out.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.4.3, Emergency Stops (Stab Braking)

question: If your ABS malfunctions while driving, what should you do?
choice_a: Stop immediately and abandon the vehicle
choice_b: Drive normally since you still have regular brake functions, and get the system serviced soon
choice_c: Disconnect the trailer immediately
choice_d: Continue driving but never use the brakes again
explanation: If ABS malfunctions, the driver still has regular brakes and should drive normally, but get the system serviced soon.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.4.2, Braking with Antilock Brakes

question: What is a primary cause of brake fade or brake failure in air brake systems?
choice_a: Using the brakes too little on long downgrades
choice_b: Excessive heat from overusing the service brakes without relying on engine braking
choice_c: Keeping the air tanks too full
choice_d: Draining the air tanks too frequently
explanation: Brakes can fade or fail from excessive heat caused by using the service brakes too much and not relying on the engine braking effect; excessive heat causes chemical changes in the brake lining that reduce friction and can lead to brakes that cannot be slowed or stopped.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.4.5, Brake Fading or Failure

question: When using the proper braking technique on a long, steep downgrade, once the vehicle is in the proper low gear, how should the brakes be applied?
choice_a: Just hard enough to feel a definite slowdown, then released when speed drops about 5 mph below the safe speed
choice_b: As hard as possible continuously until reaching the bottom
choice_c: Only using the trailer hand valve
choice_d: Lightly tapped every few seconds regardless of speed
explanation: The proper technique is to apply the brakes just hard enough to feel a definite slowdown, then release the brakes when speed has been reduced to about 5 mph below the safe speed (holding the application for about three seconds), repeating this cycle as needed down the grade.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.4.6, Proper Braking Technique

question: If the low air pressure warning comes on while driving, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Continue driving normally since spring brakes will eventually stop the vehicle
choice_b: Stop and safely park the vehicle as soon as possible, since there might be an air leak
choice_c: Immediately disconnect the trailer
choice_d: Accelerate to reach a service station quickly
explanation: If the low air pressure warning comes on, the driver should stop and safely park the vehicle as soon as possible, since controlled braking is only possible while enough air remains, and it is much safer to stop while there is enough air to use the foot brakes rather than let the spring brakes apply on their own.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.4.7, Low Air Pressure

question: When should a driver avoid using the parking brakes?
choice_a: Whenever the vehicle is loaded
choice_b: When the brakes are very hot from a steep grade, or very wet in freezing temperatures
choice_c: Whenever driving in dry, warm weather
choice_d: Only when the vehicle is a straight truck
explanation: The parking brakes should not be used if the brakes are very hot (from just coming down a steep grade), since heat can damage them, or if they are very wet in freezing temperatures, since they can freeze and prevent the vehicle from moving; wheel chocks should be used instead in those situations.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.4.8, Parking Brakes

question: Why should a driver never leave a vehicle unattended without applying the parking brakes or chocking the wheels?
choice_a: It is only a suggestion with no real risk
choice_b: The vehicle might roll away and cause injury and damage
choice_c: It voids the vehicle's insurance automatically
choice_d: It triggers the ABS malfunction lamp
explanation: A driver should never leave a vehicle unattended without applying the parking brakes or chocking the wheels, since the vehicle might roll away and cause injury and damage.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 5.4.8, Parking Brakes

question: During the CDL skills test in Iowa, what does the manual state about the service brake check that differs from demonstrating other pre-trip items?
choice_a: It must be physically demonstrated by driving the vehicle at 25 mph
choice_b: It requires only a verbal description; no physical demonstration is required in Iowa
choice_c: It is skipped entirely in Iowa
choice_d: It requires a written essay instead of a verbal explanation
explanation: The Iowa CDL manual specifically notes that for the service brake check step (pulling forward at 5 mph and applying the brake to check for pulling or delayed stopping), the applicant should verbally describe only, and no physical demonstration will be required in Iowa.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 11.1.2, Air Brake or Hydraulic Brake Check (Iowa note)

question: According to the Iowa CDL manual, what happens if an applicant fails to explain and demonstrate all four parts of the air brake check correctly during the vehicle inspection test?
choice_a: It results in a minor point deduction only
choice_b: It results in an automatic failure of the CDL Vehicle Inspection test
choice_c: The examiner will simply skip that section
choice_d: It only affects the air brake endorsement, not the base license
explanation: The Iowa manual states that failure to explain and demonstrate (perform) all four parts of the air brake check correctly will result in an automatic failure of the CDL Vehicle Inspection test.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 11.1.2, Air Brake or Hydraulic Brake Check

question: During the Air Warning Device(s) Test portion of the four-part air brake check, at what pressure should the low air warning devices (buzzer, light, and flag) activate?
choice_a: Before air pressure drops below 55 psi
choice_b: Before air pressure drops below 100 psi
choice_c: Only after the parking brake pops out
choice_d: Before air pressure drops below 20 psi
explanation: As part of the four-part pre-trip air brake check, while fanning off air pressure with the foot brake, the low air warning devices (buzzer, light, and flag) should activate before air pressure drops below 55 psi.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 11.1.2, Air Brake or Hydraulic Brake Check (Air Warning Device Test)
